summary: Specifies the Initial Connection Protocol, the third-level procedure for connecting a user process, typically Telnet, to a server process, typically a logger, at another site. It describes a family of such protocols and the values for connecting Telnets to loggers. It replaced RFC 123, RFC 143 and RFC 145.

eli5.summary: This is the polite way two computers say hello and move to a private line. The first one calls a well-known number, then they switch to another so the first line is free.

subtitle: How a user process, typically Telnet, reaches a server process, typically a Logger, on another ARPANET host.

tldr.problem: A user process at one site needs a standard way to reach a server process at another site, such as a Telnet reaching a Logger, without tying up the well-known server socket.
tldr.mechanism: The user connects to a well-known server socket L. The server sends back a 32-bit even socket number S and closes that connection. Sockets S and S+1 at the server are then connected to sockets U+3 and U+2 at the user.
tldr.outcome: This is a proposal that would become official if no serious objections were raised before 2 June 71. It replaces RFC 123, RFC 143 and RFC 145.

sections.title: What an Initial Connection Protocol Is
sections.content:
This RFC specifies the third-level protocol used to connect a user process at one site with a server process at another. In the main case the user process is a Telnet and the server process is a Logger, but the RFC says there will be other cases. It describes a family of Initial Connection Protocols (ICPs) that set up one pair of connections between any user and any server, and gives the parameter values for Telnets and Loggers.

The description is at two levels: the third (user) level, which uses an ad hoc notation of calls such as Init, Listen, Send, Receive and Close, and the second (NCP) level, which uses control commands.
sections.eli5: It is the rulebook for how a program on one computer first knocks on the door of a program on another computer.

sections.title: The User-Level Exchange
sections.content:
A server process attaches a well-advertised send socket L and listens. The user process connects to L from its receive socket U, with a byte size of 32. The server sends a 32-bit even number S and closes the connection. S and its successor S+1 are the socket numbers the server will use. The final step connects server sockets S and S+1 to user sockets U+3 and U+2 respectively.

L is a send socket (odd), while S and U are receive sockets (even). Each ICP is characterized by three numbers: L and the byte sizes Bs and Bu. L must be a send socket, both sizes must be legal, and each L has only one pair of byte sizes, so two services cannot share one socket and differ only by byte size.

Moving to new sockets frees L to accept the next caller.
sections.eli5: You call the front desk number. The desk tells you a private room number and hangs up, then you both meet in the private room.

sections.title: The NCP-Level Commands
sections.content:
At the second level the same exchange uses NCP control commands: RTS and STR to match sockets, ALL to allocate, and CLS to close. The user starts with RTS from U to L. The server answers with STR, sends S as one 32-bit byte under an allocation, and both sides then issue CLS. The server and user then use RTS and STR for the pairs (S, U+3) and (S+1, U+2). Some of these steps can be swapped or run in parallel.

The specified values are message allocation m1 = 1, bit allocation b1 = 32 and byte size s1 = 32. Links are not specified. Because some hosts have difficulty sending 32-bit bytes, it is temporarily allowed to send S as four 8-bit bytes in one message. The NCP may receive RTS or STR before the local Init or Listen, so requests for idle sockets should be queued as time and space allow.
sections.eli5: The same hello is done again in the computers' own short codes: ask, answer, hang up, then set up the two new lines.

sections.title: Telnet and Logger, and Approval
sections.content:
For connecting Telnet and Logger processes the parameters are L = 1 (written X'00000001'), Bs = s3 = 8, and Bu and s2 left to the process.

The document is a proposed official protocol. It would become official if no serious objections were raised before 2 June 71; Jon Postel planned a telephone survey of Network Liaisons, and the Working Group chairman would then declare it official. It is based on RFC 123 by S. Crocker and discussions by the ICP Committee.
sections.eli5: For the everyday case of logging in to another computer, the front desk number is 1, and the private lines send one small letter at a time.
